manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Bee Collecting Nectar While Transferring PollenI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Bee Collecting Nectar While Transferring Pollen Between Flowers2. Subject: Natural Science – Biology3. Demonstration Objective: To observe and understand how a honeybee lands on blossoms of the same flowering plant species, collects nectar, and transfers pollen between flowers, thereby illustrating the biological process of pollination.II. Demonstration Materials and ConditionsFlowering plants of the same species (with visible stamens and pistils), honeybee (real observation in nature or simulated/animated demonstration), outdoor garden or greenhouse environment with sufficient light, close-up observation tools (camera or magnifier, optional).III. Demonstration Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Select a flowering plant species with multiple open blossoms. Ensure flowers are mature, with visible pollen on the anthers. Position the observation area so that the flowers are clearly visible.2. Initial Observation: Observe a honeybee approaching the flowering plant. Focus on a single bee to track its movement clearly.3. Core Demonstration Operation:   (1) The honeybee lands on the first flower, contacting the stamens while extending its proboscis to collect nectar.   (2) Pollen grains adhere to the bee’s legs and body hairs during nectar collection.   (3) The honeybee then flies to another flower of the same plant species.   (4) As the bee lands on the second flower, pollen on its body comes into contact with the stigma of the new flower.4. Continued Observation: Observe repeated movement of the honeybee between multiple flowers of the same species, noting consistent pollen transfer.5. Conclusion of Demonstration: Summarize the observed process after the bee leaves the flowers.IV. Observation of Demonstration Phenomena1. Initial State: Flowers are intact, with pollen visibly present on anthers; no bee contact yet.2. During the Demonstration: The honeybee repeatedly lands on flowers, collects nectar, and pollen grains become attached to its body.3. Resulting Phenomenon: When the bee visits subsequent flowers, pollen is deposited onto the stigmas, completing pollen transfer.V. Summary of Experimental (Biological) PrinciplesThis demonstration illustrates pollination in flowering plants. Honeybees act as pollinators by collecting nectar for food. During this process, pollen grains from the anthers stick to the bee’s hairy body. When the bee visits another flower of the same species, pollen is transferred to the stigma, enabling fertilization and subsequent seed formation. This mutualistic relationship benefits both the plant (reproduction) and the bee (nutrition).VI. Demonstration Notes1. Focus on flowers of the same species to ensure biological correctness of pollination.2. The demonstration may be simplified or accelerated for short video presentation, retaining only the core steps of landing, nectar collection, and pollen transfer.3. Avoid disturbing the bee to maintain natural behavior.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Pollination by honeybees. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: honeybee seeks nectar; pollen adheres to bee body; pollen transfers upon contact with another flower’s stigma of the same species. Phased storyline: (1) establish flowering plant with visible reproductive structures; (2) bee lands and collects nectar, contacting pollen; (3) pollen visibly attaches to bee; (4) bee moves to another flower of same species; (5) pollen contacts stigma, completing transfer. Visibility constraints: close-up or clear perspective on bee–flower contact points to verify pollen movement and causal sequence.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Formation of Ammonium Chloride Particulate from Ammonia and Hydrogen ChlorideI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Formation of Ammonium Chloride Particulate by Gas Diffusion2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that when ammonia vapor and hydrogen chloride vapor diffuse and meet in air, they react to form fine ammonium chloride particulate, simulating secondary aerosol formation in the atmosphere.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass chamber with two opposite openings or inlets; ammonia source (concentrated ammonia solution with cotton or ammonia gas generator); hydrogen chloride source (concentrated hydrochloric acid with cotton or HCl gas generator); tweezers; rubber stoppers or lids; camera with fixed focus and tripod; protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear glass chamber on a stable surface. Fix the camera on a tripod facing the chamber and lock focus and exposure for time-lapse recording.2. Gas Placement: Using tweezers, place an ammonia-soaked cotton at one side inlet of the chamber and a hydrogen chloride–soaked cotton at the opposite side inlet.3. Release and Recording: Simultaneously open or unseal both sides to allow ammonia vapor and hydrogen chloride vapor to diffuse into the chamber. Start time-lapse recording without moving the camera.4. Observation Period: Allow the gases to diffuse and mix naturally in the chamber for a short period until visible particulate appears.5. Completion: Seal the chamber, stop recording, and ventilate the area safely after observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The chamber is clear and transparent with no visible particles.2. During Diffusion: Invisible gases spread from opposite sides toward the center of the chamber.3. Mixing Zone: A white, smoke-like particulate gradually appears where the two gases meet.4. Final State: The white particulate becomes denser at the interface region, forming a visible band or cloud of ammonium chloride.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAmmonia (NH3) and hydrogen chloride (HCl) are gaseous substances that diffuse through air. When they meet, they undergo an acid–base reaction forming solid ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) as fine particulate matter. This process models the formation of secondary inorganic aerosols in the atmosphere.Core Reaction: NH3(g) + HCl(g) → NH4Cl(s)VI. Experimental Precautions1. Perform the experiment in a well-ventilated area or fume hood.2. Avoid direct inhalation of gases; wear goggles and gloves.3. Ensure the camera remains fixed to maintain consistent observation.4. Dispose of chemical materials according to safety regulations.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Secondary aerosol formation through gas-phase diffusion and acid–base reaction, assuming basic gas diffusion and visible particulate formation without complex atmospheric dynamics. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) clear, static glass chamber with fixed camera view; (2) release of ammonia and hydrogen chloride from opposite sides; (3) invisible diffusion toward the center; (4) emergence of a white particulate band where gases meet; (5) gradual intensification of particulate during time-lapse, with no camera movement and consistent spatial perspective for verification.
